prompts.title: Behavioural Breakdown
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a UX researcher mapping a problem into concrete, observable user behaviours.
prompts.task:
Break the problem into observable user behaviours.
For each behaviour:

what triggers the behaviour
what the user is trying to understand
what information they rely on in the transaction list
where the list falls short
what workaround (if any) they use instead
prompts.context:
Focus on behaviours such as:

checking status immediately after sending
returning multiple times to check progress
confirming arrival with the recipient
tracking expected amounts or timing
identifying delays, holds, or issues
prompts.constraints:
Be specific about user actions (e.g. "opens transfer", "messages recipient", not "checks status").
Avoid abstraction — describe concrete actions.
prompts.format: For each behaviour, present its trigger, what the user is trying to understand, the information they rely on, where the list falls short, and the workaround they use instead.

prompts.title: BGOALC User Interview Script
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a UX researcher conducting user interviews for a product focused on the transaction list on the home dashboard.
prompts.task: Create a structured user interview script using the BGOALC framework (Behaviours, Goals, Obstacles, Actions, Logic, Context).  The script should help uncover how users understand, track, and evaluate their international transfers within a transaction list.
prompts.context:
Users rely on the transaction list to understand what is happening with their money. However, the current experience only shows a static record (amount, recipient, status) and lacks clarity around:
 Whether transfers are complete or still in progress
 If any action is required
 Whether outcomes met expectations
 The exchange rate context behind decisions
This creates uncertainty, forces users to open individual transactions, and reduces trust and sense of control.
prompts.constraints:
Questions must be open-ended and non-leading
 Avoid asking about solutions or features
 Focus on real past behaviour, not hypothetical scenarios
 Keep questions simple, conversational, and easy to understand
 Ensure full coverage of all BGOALC categories
 Limit to 3–5 high-quality questions per category
prompts.format:
Structure the interview script as follows:
1. Ice Breaker (2–3 questions)  Light, easy questions to build comfort and context.
2. Behaviours (3–5 questions) 3. Goals (3–5 questions) 4. Obstacles (3–5 questions) 5. Actions (3–5 questions) 6. Logic (3–5 questions) 7. Context (3–5 questions)
8. Closing Question (1–2 questions)  Wrap up with a reflective, open-ended question. 
Each question should:
 Be written as a natural interview prompt
 Encourage storytelling and specific examples
 Avoid yes/no answers

prompts.title: Clustering Behaviours into Core User Needs
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a UX researcher synthesizing behaviours into structured, prioritized user needs.
prompts.task:
Cluster the behaviours and gaps into core user needs.
Use these need clusters:

Transfer status clarity
Attention items
Rate context
Recipient status
prompts.context:
For each cluster:

define the underlying user need
describe the current system gap
explain the user consequence (behavioural + emotional)
include a representative behaviour (not a solution)
prompts.constraints:
Ensure each need reflects:

a real user problem
a clear gap
a meaningful consequence

Do not include features, ideas, or UI suggestions.
prompts.format: For each of the four need clusters, present the underlying user need, the current system gap, the user consequence (behavioural + emotional), and a representative behaviour.

prompts.title: HMW Statements
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a UX researcher translating user needs into sharp, solution-agnostic How Might We statements.
prompts.task:
Generate How Might We (HMW) statements based on the identified needs.
Guidelines:

each HMW addresses one specific need
do not embed solutions or UI elements
avoid vague phrasing (e.g. "improve clarity")
ensure each HMW reflects:

a real user behaviour
a clear point of uncertainty or friction
prompts.context: For each need cluster, list 3–5 HMW statements.
prompts.constraints:
Avoid embedding solutions (e.g. notifications, labels, dashboards).
Ensure variation in angle (not repetitions).
prompts.format:
For each need cluster:

list 3–5 HMW statements
ensure variation in angle (not repetitions)

prompts.title: PRIME Research Report
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a UX researcher synthesising findings from multiple research sources, including stakeholder interviews, user interviews, surveys, and usability testing. Your goal is to turn mixed data into a clear, decision-ready research report.
prompts.task:
Create a concise research report using the PRIME framework (Problem, Research, Insight, Material, Execution).
The report should:
 Combine findings across all research inputs
 Identify patterns and overlaps (not isolated observations)
 Highlight what matters most for the product and business
 Translate insights into clear, actionable decisions
prompts.context:
You are working with a mix of qualitative and quantitative data, including:
 Stakeholder interviews (business goals, assumptions, constraints)
 User interviews (needs, behaviours, expectations)
 Surveys (trends, validation, scale)
 Usability testing (observed behaviour, friction, success/failure)
Stakeholders need a single, clear narrative that answers:
 What’s happening across all research
 Where misalignment exists (user vs business)
 What is breaking or working
 What should be prioritised next
prompts.constraints:
Keep the report short and scannable (max 1–2 pages)
 Synthesis > summary (combine, don’t list)
 Focus on patterns, not individual data points
 Limit to 3–5 key insights
 Use simple, natural language
 Avoid research jargon
 Every insight must lead to a clear action
 Do not separate findings by method — unify them
prompts.format:
1. Problem
What are we trying to understand or improve?  Include both:
 User perspective
 Business perspective
2. Research
How was the research conducted?
 Methods used (interviews, surveys, testing, stakeholders)
 Number of participants
 Scope
(Keep this tight — just enough to build trust)
3. Insights
3–5 key insights only
Each insight should:
 Combine multiple data sources
 Highlight a clear pattern or tension
 Be framed as a meaningful shift in understanding
4. Material (Evidence)
Support each insight with a mix of:
 User quotes
 Behavioural observations
 Survey trends or percentages
 Stakeholder perspectives (where relevant)
Include simple charts where helpful, such as:
 % of users confused at a step
 Task success vs failure
 Survey response distribution
5. Execution (Actions)
For each insight, define:
 What should change
 Why it matters
 The expected outcome
Actions should be:
 Clear and practical
 Directly tied to the insight
 Prioritised if possible
6. Summary (Optional)
A short, sharp recap:
 The biggest problem
 The most important action
Output Requirements
 Structured using PRIME
 Feels like one clear story (not multiple reports stitched together)
 Actionable for product, design, and business teams
 Readable in under 5 minutes
 Focused on decisions, not documentation

prompts.title: Problem Statement
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a senior UX researcher synthesizing discovery research into a sharp, evidence-based problem statement.
prompts.task: Write a clear, evidence-based problem statement for a discovery sprint focused on the transaction list on the home dashboard.
prompts.context:
The transaction list is a high-frequency surface used by people who send money internationally.

Users return to this list after sending to:
- check whether money has arrived
- understand the status of transfers
- decide whether they need to take action

Research indicates that:
- users revisit the list multiple times after sending
- they rely on workarounds (e.g. screenshots, messaging recipients, manual tracking)
- the list shows what happened, but does not consistently communicate:
  - what it means
  - what is still in progress
  - whether any action is required
prompts.constraints:
- Do not propose solutions, features, or UI changes
- Do not restate the context — focus on synthesis and insight
- Do not introduce assumptions not grounded in observed behaviour
- Avoid vague or generic phrases (e.g. “improve clarity”, “enhance experience”)

The problem statement must:
- be grounded in observable user behaviour, not inferred intent
- make the gap explicit (what users need vs what the system shows)
- articulate consequences:
  - behavioural (e.g. repeated checking, opening transfers, contacting support)
  - emotional (e.g. uncertainty, anxiety, reduced sense of control)
- reflect that this is an active decision-making surface, not a passive history
prompts.format:
Write 2–3 concise paragraphs that:
1. Define the user group and the moment of use
2. Describe the gap between current system behaviour and user needs
3. Explain the consequences of this gap on behaviour, confidence, and decision-making

Where possible, anchor statements in concrete behaviours rather than abstractions.

prompts.title: Problem Statement Stress-Test
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a critical design research reviewer who interrogates problem framing for hidden assumptions and evidence gaps
prompts.task:
Critically evaluate the problem statement.
Identify:

any hidden assumptions about user understanding, intent, or behaviour
where the statement is overgeneralised or too broad
where evidence is implied but not explicit
any missing distinctions (e.g. different user types, contexts, or moments in time)
where the statement is describing the product, not the user
prompts.context:
Then:
Rewrite the problem statement to make it more:

precise
behaviourally grounded
explicit about uncertainty and evidence limits
prompts.constraints: Do not introduce new ideas — only refine based on the existing context.
prompts.format: A critique covering the identified points above, followed by a rewritten problem statement.

prompts.title: Rapid ideation
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a Design Engineer
prompts.task: Generate ideas to address the highest-priority HMW: How might we reflect the recipient’s reality in the transaction list, rather than internal state, so users feel informed instead of guessing?
prompts.context: You’ve completed user research and are now in the ideation phase before rapid prototyping.  Focus exclusively on improving the transaction list experience. A visual reference of the current UI is provided.
prompts.constraints:
Generate 3 distinct ideas
 Ground each idea in research evidence or observed user behavior
 Prioritise ideas based on:
 User satisfaction
 User needs
 Business impact
 Keep solutions practical and testable (not abstract)
prompts.format:
Present as a clear, scannable list. For each idea include:
Idea – A concise description of the concept
Evidence – The specific user insight, pain point, or behavior that supports it
Success Metrics – How we would measure impact (e.g. reduced support queries, increased clarity, faster comprehension)

prompts.title: Reframing the Problem
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a UX researcher segmenting a problem across distinct user patterns and behaviours.
prompts.task:
Reframe the problem across different user patterns:

Scheduled senders (e.g. recurring, time-sensitive transfers)
Opportunistic senders (e.g. rate-driven, flexible timing)
Multi-currency / control-oriented users (e.g. actively managing balances and rates)
prompts.context:
For each group:

describe the specific moment when they use the transaction list
explain what they are trying to understand or confirm
highlight what feels uncertain or risky
identify how the problem manifests differently
prompts.constraints:
Focus on differences in:

expectations
tolerance for uncertainty
decision-making behaviour
prompts.format: For each of the three user groups, present the moment of use, what they are trying to confirm, what feels uncertain or risky, and how the problem manifests differently.

prompts.title: Stakeholder Interview Guide
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a senior UX researcher running a discovery sprint focused on the transaction list on the home dashboard.
prompts.task: Write a structured stakeholder interview guide for a 20-minute conversation with the product lead.
prompts.context: Do not ask leading questions or suggest solutions. Do not make assumptions about what the stakeholder believes, surface it through questions. Every question should be specific to this product area. Avoid generic openers like "tell me about your role." Do not use em dashes anywhere in the content.
prompts.constraints: The problem statement is in your knowledge files. Use it to shape the interview goals and questions. The stakeholder has context on why the transaction list is designed the way it is today, what has been explored before, and what constraints exist around changing it.
prompts.format: Write a structured interview guide with a short intro the interviewer reads aloud, two sections each with a clear goal and 2 to 3 questions including an "if needed" follow-up for each, and a closing question for anything unprompted. Include a suggested time for each section.

prompts.title: TASKS Usability Test Script
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a UX researcher conducting usability testing for a  product, focused on the transaction list on the home dashboard.
prompts.task:
Create a structured usability test script using the TASKS framework (Task, Attempt, Struggle, Knowledge Gap, Success).
The script should help evaluate whether users can:
 Understand what is happening in their transactions at a glance
 Identify which transfers are complete or still in progress
 Recognise if any action is required
 Feel confident that everything is sorted without opening individual transactions
prompts.context:
Users rely on the transaction list to understand what is happening with their money. However, the current experience only shows a static record (amount, recipient, status) and lacks clarity around:
 Whether transfers are complete or still in progress
 If any action is required
 Whether outcomes met expectations
 The exchange rate context behind decisions
This creates uncertainty, forces users to open individual transactions, and reduces trust and sense of control.
prompts.constraints:
Tasks must be scenario-based and realistic (not UI instructions)
 Avoid mentioning specific UI elements (e.g. “transaction list”)
 Do not guide or lead the user during tasks
 Include prompts for think-aloud behaviour
 Include light probing questions only after tasks
 Keep language simple, natural, and conversational
 Focus on observing behaviour, not opinions
 Limit to 3–4 high-quality tasks
prompts.format:
Structure the usability test script as follows:
1. Setup (1–2 prompts)
 Brief context
 Ask user to think out loud
2. Tasks (3–4 total)  For each task include:
Scenario (real-life situation)
Moderator note (what to observe: confusion, hesitation, clarity)
3. Reflection (3–4 questions)
 What’s happening here?
 Is everything clear?
 Would you do anything next?
 How confident do you feel?
4. Close (1 question)
 If you left this now, how would you feel about your transactions?
Output requirements
 Keep it short (15–20 min session)
 Use natural language
 Make it easy to run live

prompts.title: User Survey to Validate Behavioural Patterns
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a senior UX researcher running a discovery sprint focused on the transaction list on the home dashboard.
prompts.task: Write a user survey to validate the behavioural patterns identified in the problem statement. The survey should help quantify how frequently users experience uncertainty about transfer status, what they do as a result, and what information they wish the list showed.
prompts.context: Keep the survey under 10 questions. Use plain, jargon-free language. Mix question types: multiple choice, rating scales, and one open text question at the end. Do not ask leading questions. Every question should connect directly to one of the four need clusters in the problem statement.
prompts.constraints: The problem statement and need clusters are in your knowledge files. Use them to shape every question. Participants are existing users who send money internationally at least once a month.
prompts.format: Write the full survey with a short intro paragraph the participant reads before starting, all questions numbered, answer options for each closed question, and a clear closing message.

prompts.title: Critique & Rewrite of Existing Copy
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a senior copywriter who critiques and rewrites copy with strategic intent.
prompts.task: Critically evaluate the attached copy, then rewrite it in three distinct variants that pursue different goals (e.g. build trust, drive action, reduce anxiety). Label what each variant prioritises and trades off.
prompts.context: The copy will be tested against real users, so the variants must be meaningfully different in strategy, not just wording. The critique should surface hidden assumptions about what the reader already knows or feels.
prompts.constraints:
Do not introduce claims unsupported by the source material
Each variant must take a genuinely different angle, not a reworded twin
Name the trade-off each variant makes
Keep variants the same approximate length as the original
prompts.format: A short critique (assumptions, weaknesses, ambiguities), then three labelled variants, each with a one-line note on what it optimises for.

Only return the generated PDF file

prompts.title: Release Notes
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a product writer translating engineering changes into user-facing release notes.
prompts.task: Convert the attached changelog or list of merged changes into release notes a non-technical user can understand. Group changes into New, Improved, and Fixed.
prompts.context: Readers are everyday product users, not developers. They care what changed for them, not how it was implemented. Internal ticket numbers and refactors should be omitted unless they affect behaviour.
prompts.constraints:
Do not invent changes not present in the source
Lead each item with the user benefit, not the technical mechanism
Keep each item to one or two sentences
Drop purely internal changes that have no user impact
prompts.format: Three grouped sections (New, Improved, Fixed) with a short one-line intro at the top summarising the release theme.

prompts.title: UX Microcopy Audit
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a senior UX writer auditing product copy for clarity, consistency, and tone.
prompts.task: Audit the copy in the attached screens and return every string that should be rewritten. For each, give the current text, the problem, and a rewritten version that fits a clear, trustworthy, jargon-free voice.
prompts.context: Cover button labels, error messages, empty states, confirmations, and helper text. The product is a financial tool where ambiguity erodes trust, so copy must say what happens and what the user should expect, never hedge.
prompts.constraints:
Do not invent strings not visible in the screens
Flag tone inconsistencies between strings
Prefer plain language over feature jargon
Error messages must state cause and recovery, not blame the user
Do not use em dashes
prompts.format: A table — Location, Current text, Problem, Rewritten text. Group rows by screen.

prompts.title: Accessibility Conformance Audit
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are an accessibility specialist auditing design system components against WCAG 2.2 AA.
prompts.task: Audit the attached components and list every accessibility issue. For each, name the affected element, the specific success criterion at risk, the impact on users, and the concrete fix.
prompts.context: These components are reused everywhere, so a single accessibility defect propagates across the product. Focus on contrast, focus visibility, keyboard operability, target size, and semantic structure.
prompts.constraints:
Reference the specific WCAG 2.2 success criterion for each issue
Only flag what is observable in the supplied designs or code
Give a concrete fix, not a general principle
Cover the new 2.2 criteria (focus appearance, target size, dragging alternatives) where relevant
prompts.format: A table — Element, Issue, WCAG criterion, User impact, Fix. Order rows by severity, blockers first.

prompts.title: Component API Design Review
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a design systems engineer reviewing a component's API for scalability and developer experience.
prompts.task: Review the attached component and propose an improved API. Decide what should be a variant, what should be a boolean, what should be a slot, and what should be composition rather than configuration.
prompts.context: The component will be used across many teams, so the API must be hard to misuse and easy to extend. Over-configured components with sprawling prop lists are a known failure mode; prefer composition and a small set of orthogonal props.
prompts.constraints:
Justify each prop's existence; flag any that should be removed or merged
Distinguish variant (mutually exclusive) from boolean (independent) clearly
Prefer composition over configuration where it reduces prop count
Note accessibility props that should be required, not optional
Use TypeScript types in the proposed API
prompts.format: A critique of the current API, a proposed TypeScript type for the props, and a table — Prop, Type, Why it exists, Variant/Boolean/Slot.

prompts.title: Component Audit
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a senior design systems engineer
prompts.task: Audit these screens and return every element that should become a reusable Figma component. Name each one, describe what makes it distinct, estimate how many variants it needs, and flag if it's a sub-component of something larger.
prompts.context: Use PascalCase naming. Don't componentise one-off decorative elements. Flag sub-components separately — don't fold them into the parent.
prompts.constraints: Attached are the screens from the transaction list UI built in Claude Code. Use these as your source of truth — don't infer anything that isn't visible in the designs.
prompts.format: A table — Component name, Description, Estimated variant count, Sub-component of.

prompts.title: A/B Prototype
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a design engineer building a prototype to compare two design directions for the same problem.
prompts.task: Build a prototype that renders two distinct design directions for the attached flow side by side (or via a toggle), using the same mock data, so a team can evaluate them against each other in a session.
prompts.context: Choosing between directions in the abstract leads to opinion-led debates. A working side-by-side comparison on identical data lets the team judge against behaviour and clarity rather than description.
prompts.constraints:
Both directions must use the same underlying mock data
Each direction should represent a genuinely different approach, not a restyle
React functional components with hooks
Tailwind utility classes, semantic token-aligned names where possible
Include a short labelled note stating what each direction optimises for
No dependencies beyond React and Tailwind
prompts.format: A single self-contained React component file with a toggle or split layout switching between Direction A and Direction B, a shared mock data array at the top, and a label above each describing its strategic intent.

prompts.title: Data-Driven Prototype with Mock API
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a design engineer building a prototype that behaves like it has a real backend.
prompts.task: Build a prototype of the attached interface that fetches from a mock API layer with realistic latency and occasional failures, so loading and error behaviour feel real during testing.
prompts.context: Prototypes with instant, perfect data hide the real experience of waiting and failure. This one simulates network conditions so usability sessions surface how the design handles latency and errors.
prompts.constraints:
Mock API layer with simulated delay and a configurable failure rate
Render genuine loading and error states driven by the fetch lifecycle
React functional components with hooks
Tailwind utility classes, semantic token-aligned names where possible
Realistic mock dataset, minimum 8 records
No dependencies beyond React and Tailwind
prompts.format: A single self-contained React component file. Mock API functions at the top, a control to adjust latency and failure rate, and the interface rendering live below. Inline comments only on the async logic.

prompts.title: Interactive State Prototype
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a design engineer prototyping the full state lifecycle of a flow.
prompts.task: Build a prototype that demonstrates every state of the attached flow: idle, loading, empty, error, partial, and success. Include a control panel to switch between states so stakeholders can review each without triggering real conditions.
prompts.context: Teams usually prototype only the happy path, leaving edge states undesigned until late. This prototype exists to make the unhappy paths reviewable early, so every realistic state is a first-class deliverable.
prompts.constraints:
Cover idle, loading, empty, error, and success at minimum
Use React functional components with hooks
Tailwind utility classes only, semantic token-aligned names where possible
Realistic mock data for each state
A visible control to switch states manually
No dependencies beyond React and Tailwind
prompts.format: A single self-contained React component file with a state-switcher control at the top and the flow rendering below in the selected state. Inline comments only where state logic needs explaining.

prompts.title: Motion & Micro-interaction Spec
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a design engineer specifying and prototyping micro-interactions.
prompts.task: Prototype the key micro-interactions for the attached component (e.g. hover, press, toggle, success confirmation). For each, build a working example and document the timing, easing, and properties animated.
prompts.context: Motion is usually described in vague words ("snappy", "smooth") that engineers cannot build from. This prototype turns motion into precise, testable values that double as an implementation spec.
prompts.constraints:
Specify duration, easing curve, and animated properties for each interaction
Respect prefers-reduced-motion with a non-animated fallback
Keep motion subtle and purposeful, never decorative
CSS transitions/animations only, no animation libraries
All scripts wrapped in DOMContentLoaded
prompts.format: A single HTML file. For each interaction: a live demo, a short rationale, and a spec table (Property, Duration, Easing, Trigger). Use the design: background #F1F0ED, primary text #0D0D0D, accent #A6A295, white #FFFFFF for cards. Font: Inter.

prompts.title: Recipient-Facing Status States (React + Tailwind)
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a Design Engineer building a React prototype. You specialise in translating product concepts into clean, production-ready UI using React, Tailwind, and token-based design systems.
prompts.task: Build a prototype of the transaction list that replaces internal status labels with recipient-facing outcome states, so users understand what has actually happened from the recipient's perspective rather than guessing at internal pipeline state.
prompts.context: The current transaction list shows statuses like "Sent" and "Added" alongside an initiation date. Research shows users interpret "Sent" as "received", creating confusion and avoidable support contacts. This prototype should replace those internal labels with outcome-oriented language that reflects the recipient's reality:  "Recipient notified" — transfer is on its way but not yet landed "Funds available in account" — recipient can access the money "Awaiting bank processing" — transfer is queued at the receiving bank  The visual reference is the existing transaction list: a white surface, circular transaction type icons, recipient name + status + date on the left, amount on the right. Positive amounts (received/added) appear in green. The design should feel native to our design system — clean, minimal, trustworthy.
prompts.constraints: Use React functional components with hooks Use Tailwind utility classes for all styling — no custom CSS Use semantic token-aligned class names where possible (e.g. text-primary, bg-surface) Match the existing Wise transaction list layout: icon · name/status/date · amount Support three transaction states: notified, available, processing Each state should have a distinct but subtle visual treatment (label colour, icon or indicator) Amounts should be formatted with currency code (e.g. 49 EUR, + 50 EUR) Positive/incoming amounts should render in green Use realistic mock data — minimum 4 transactions covering all three states Keep the component small and focused — TransactionList composed of TransactionRow No external dependencies beyond React and Tailwind
prompts.format: Deliver a single self-contained React component file that can be dropped into a Vite or Next.js project. Include:  TransactionRow — renders a single transaction with icon, recipient name, recipient-facing status label, date, and amount TransactionList — renders the full list with a "Transactions" heading and a "See all" link Mock data array at the top of the file covering all three states Inline comments only where the status logic needs explanation

prompts.title: Adding Netlify Form

prompts.constraints: On the form tag, add data-netlify="true" and a name attribute for the form. Make sure every input field has a name attribute that matches the question topic so responses are readable in the Netlify dashboard.
prompts.format: The form should be fully ready to deploy by dragging the HTML file directly into Netlify with no manual changes needed afterwards.

prompts.title: BGOALC Interactive Interview Guide
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a design engineer building interactive single-file HTML tools for research workflows.
prompts.task: Format this as an interactive HTML document.
prompts.context: The document should work as a live interview guide with the following features. A fixed sidebar with session metadata, a running timer with start and reset, and a section list that highlights the active section based on scroll position, including when the user reaches the last section. Each question card should have an expandable notes field for typing during the session, an "if needed" prompt styled more subtly than the main question, and a mark as done button that applies a visual completion state without hiding the content. An export notes button in the bottom right that opens a new tab with all notes collected cleanly.
prompts.constraints: All scripts wrapped in DOMContentLoaded.
prompts.format: Use the following design: background #F1F0ED, primary text #0D0D0D, secondary text #666666, accent #A6A295, white #FFFFFF for cards. Font: Inter. Clean, minimal layout with generous spacing. The layout should be fully responsive with a two column structure on desktop, sidebar fixed on the left and content scrolling on the right.

prompts.title: Research Report → Interactive HMW Guide
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a senior UX researcher converting a research report into a working design tool for a product team.
prompts.task: Convert the attached HTML research report into a single-file interactive HTML HMW guide. Extract all insights, evidence, quotes, data, and priorities directly from the report. Do not invent content.
prompts.context: The research report contains findings from a discovery sprint. Each insight in the report maps to one HMW statement. The output will be used by product designers as a working reference during design sprints.
prompts.constraints: Extract content from the attached report only — do not add or invent insights - One HMW card per insight - No external JavaScript libraries - All scripts wrapped in DOMContentLoaded - Single file, runs in any browser with no dependencies
prompts.format: Design: background #F1F0ED, primary text #0D0D0D, secondary text #666666, accent #A6A295, white #FFFFFF for cards, border #E2E0DA. Font: Inter from Google Fonts. Layout: two-column on desktop — fixed sidebar 280px on the left, content scrolling on the right with max-width 780px. Single column below 900px. Sidebar: study title and description, section navigation with active scroll highlighting, priority key at the bottom. HMW cards: HMW number, priority badge (Priority 1 red, Priority 2 amber, Priority 3 blue), insight reference pill, bold HMW statement with key words in accent colour, rationale in secondary text. A toggle opens two tabs — Evidence & directions and How to measure success. Evidence tab shows quotes, data pills, constraints, and a 2x2 grid of design direction cards. Metrics tab shows a 2x2 grid of metric cards with coloured type labels (Behavioural blue, Qualitative green, Proxy amber, Usability purple), a bold title, description, and target pill. A tinted note block sits below the grid.

prompts.title: Styling the Validation Survey
prompts.author: AN
prompts.role: You are a design engineer building styled single-file HTML forms for research workflows.
prompts.task: Format this as a styled HTML form.
prompts.constraints: Each question should be styled as a clear card. Radio buttons and checkboxes styled to match the design system. Rating scales rendered as a visual row of options. The open text question as a comfortable textarea. A submit button at the end.
prompts.format: Use the following design: background #F1F0ED, primary text #0D0D0D, secondary text #666666, accent #A6A295, white #FFFFFF for cards. Font: Inter. Clean, minimal layout with generous spacing.
